title: VII: The Governor’s Hall

teacherSummary.text: Hearing that the magistrates may take Pearl, Hester brings gloves to Governor Bellingham's mansion. In a polished breastplate she sees the letter grotesquely magnified. Pearl, dressed in scarlet, cries for a red rose in the garden.

segments.script: Bellingham was governor several times; the narrator notes the English gentleman's attempt to make an English garden in rough soil. In authority's mirror the letter dominates who Hester is. Setting: Governor Bellingham's mansion, its glittering stucco and the convex breastplate that magnifies the letter. Symbolism: In the armor's curved mirror the scarlet letter appears "in exaggerated and gigantic proportions." Characterization: Bellingham's English garden fails: cabbages and pumpkin vines replace ornament. Watch for the scarlet letter: The embroidered "A" changes meaning as the town and the reader watch it: adultery, then "Able," then something like "Angel," and finally an emblem Hester chooses to keep. In this chapter: “went, one day, to the mansion of Governor Bellingham, with a pair of gloves, which she had fringed and embroidered to his” (VII: The Governor’s Hall, paragraph 1).

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “the scarlet letter was represented in exaggerated and gigantic proportions, so as to be greatly the most prominent feature of her appearance” slowly and put it in my own words: In the governor's polished armor, the scarlet letter appears hugely exaggerated, the most prominent part of Hester's appearance. Next, craft. I notice the distortion: the curved armor makes the letter swallow her image. The strongest word is “exaggerated”: it shows how her shame dominates how others see her. Then, effect. What does the reflection in the armor show? My answer: The armor reflects society's view: the letter has replaced her as a person; Hawthorne shows how a label can overshadow identity.
